title: Nobody Told You the Suit Was a System. That's Why Yours Doesn't Fit.
stand: Buy the jacket for the shoulders and the trouser for the break. Everything else is alteration, and alteration is where the money actually goes.

hero.alt: Paris Pullen in a navy pinstripe double-breasted suit and gold tie

body: A suit is not a single purchase. It behaves like one at the register and like a system everywhere after, which is the first thing that confuses a man buying his first genuinely good one — he expects the jacket to fit the way it looked on the hanger, and it never does, because the hanger was not built like him.

Shoulders are the one structural element a tailor cannot meaningfully change after the fact. Everything below the collarbone can be taken in, let out, shortened, reshaped. The shoulder seam is closer to permanent, which is why it is the only measurement worth obsessing over before the fabric is even cut.

The trouser earns the same obsession for a different reason — the break. Too much fabric pooling at the ankle reads as inherited, not chosen. Too little reads as outgrown. The correct break is a narrow window, and it is the detail a well-trained eye clocks before it registers the fabric, the cut, or the color.
PQ::Everything else is alteration, and alteration is where the money actually goes.

This is the part nobody explains at the point of sale. The suit on the rack was never meant to be worn as sold. It is a starting position, a rough draft in cloth, and the real cost of owning it well is not the tag price but the three or four visits to a tailor afterward — taking in the waist, softening the sleeve, moving a button half an inch, because half an inch is the entire difference between a suit that fits and one that merely covers.

Men who skip this step are easy to spot in any room, and not for a reason they'd want pointed out. The fabric can be extraordinary and the fit can still be wrong, and a wrong fit on expensive cloth reads worse than a right fit on modest cloth — it announces money spent without judgment applied.

The system extends past the suit itself. A shirt collar that doesn't sit correctly against a jacket lapel undoes both. A shoe that fights the trouser break undoes the whole line from the knee down. None of these pieces were designed in isolation, and buying them that way is how a closet fills with expensive items that never once look like they belong to the same wardrobe.

Treat the first good suit as tuition, not a purchase. What it teaches — shoulder first, break second, alteration budget built in from day one — is the only part of the transaction that pays dividends on every suit bought after it.

title: Karma Automotive's Best-Kept Secret Isn't the Car. It's Who's Running It.
stand: There are three Black executives currently running an American car company. I went and found one of them — he'd rather talk to me about torque than the milestone.

hero.alt: A Karma Automotive coupe on an auto-show floor

body: I'll level with you: I didn't expect to be writing about Karma. Every valet I've handed one of these to has gotten the badge wrong at least once, and the company doesn't seem bothered by it. Neither, at this point, am I. There's a particular kind of quiet I've come to respect in a car that isn't fishing for a second look.

Here's the part that doesn't make it into the brochure, and the part I went digging for the second something felt off: Karma exists because a Chinese industrial conglomerate, Wanxiang, bought what was left of Fisker's bankruptcy in 2014 and rebuilt the whole operation out in Southern California. That's just the record, no spin from me. What actually held my attention wasn't the ownership. It was who they handed the keys to.

The man running it is Marques McCammon — mechanical engineer, NC A&T undergrad, Michigan for grad school, cut his teeth on the Dodge Neon SRT-4 and the Saleen S302 back when those names meant something at a bar, ran Ricardo's entire automotive business across North America, then went and figured out how software should actually run a car over at Intel's Wind River shop. He's also, by most honest counts, one of three Black men currently running an American car company. I had to go find that myself — he doesn't lead with it. His résumé does enough talking on its own.
PQA::Nobody else does it the way we do.||Marques McCammon||President, Karma Automotive

His actual pitch to me had nothing to do with any of that, and I think that's deliberate. He's put Karma above the entire EV argument the rest of the industry's stuck having. Not chasing Tesla's numbers, not Rivian's utility angle, not Lucid's range war. He's building for the guy dropping $200K to $500K who wants something closer to bespoke tailoring than a gadget with a battery bolted in. Software-defined on purpose — built around one owner, not averaged out across a hundred thousand of them.
IMG::0
IMG::1

You feel that instinct the second you look at the Kaveya — the super-coupe still making the concept-car rounds. Doors that open like they're unfolding an idea instead of announcing themselves, a steering yoke shaped like nothing else on the road right now. It doesn't photograph aggressive. It photographs like it already knows it doesn't need to try.

But that's the preview. The one I'd actually tell you to go put a deposit on this week is the Revero GT — anchored this whole brand since the Fisker days, quietly rebuilt around it twice since. I'm not going to just repeat a spec sheet at you here, though I'll give you the numbers below. Guys who've actually driven it keep wanting to keep it. That tells you more than a brochure ever will.

Range Extender + Electric Drive"], ["Combined Output", "536 HP / 550 LB-FT"], ["Battery", "28 kWh"], ["Electric Range", "80 MI"], ["Total Range", "360 MI"], ["0-60 MPH", "4.5 SEC"], ["Top Speed", "125 MPH"], ["Kerb Weight", "5,062 LBS"], ["Length", "199.4 IN"], ["Starting Price", "$124,099"]], "cta_label": "Find Out More", "cta_url": "https://karmaautomotive.com/revero/", "cta_title": "Karma Revero GT", "image": 2}

None of that changes the math I keep coming back to. Karma was never fighting for the guy who wants applause at the valet stand. It's for the one who already had that applause, decided it wasn't the point, and went looking for a car that agrees with him instead of performing for the room. What's actually changed is who's making that bet pay off — and his name is about as unfamiliar to most buyers as the badge on the hood.

That might be the most honest way I can put the whole thing to you. Karma isn't selling you a badge that explains itself, and it isn't run by a guy who needs credit for doing the work. It's a bet — car and man both — that the details do more convincing than the name ever could. I'm inclined to agree with it.

title: Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen Has One Rule Nobody Talks About
stand: Every man in that film is underestimated by someone in the first ten minutes and finishes the movie having made them regret it. That is the whole genre, done properly.

hero.alt: Official poster for Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen (2019)

body: There's a genre of British crime film that lives or dies on one specific trick — letting every character look, for the first several minutes, like exactly what a lazier film would have made them permanently. The stoner looks disposable. The posh one looks soft. The retired gangster looks retired. Guy Ritchie's The Gentlemen spends its whole runtime proving that first impression was the joke, not the plot.

What makes it worth revisiting past the plot mechanics is the class commentary sitting quietly underneath the caper — old aristocracy and new money circling the same territory, each side certain the other doesn't understand how things are really done, both occasionally right. The film never explains this directly. It just keeps putting men who misjudge each other's competence in the same room and letting the misjudgment cost someone something.
PQ::Every man in that film is underestimated by someone in the first ten minutes and finishes the movie having made them regret it.

That structure — the quiet man mistaken for harmless, correcting the record without raising his voice to do it — is the entire appeal of the genre when it's done well, and most attempts at it get the tone wrong in one direction or the other. Too much menace and it stops being fun. Too little and there's nothing at stake when the correction finally lands.
IMG::0

Ritchie's version threads that needle mostly by refusing to let anyone stay underestimated for long. The moment a character's real capability surfaces, the film moves on immediately instead of lingering on the reveal, which is a more confident choice than it sounds — it trusts the audience to have been paying attention instead of needing the point explained twice.

It plays on a screen here in a room built for exactly this kind of thing, the sort of space where a film gets watched at low volume with a drink in hand and half the room's attention, and it holds up fine under those conditions, which not every prestige crime picture manages. Some films need the theater's silence to work. This one is comfortable being the background to a good night, and comes forward when it earns it.

What sticks longest isn't any single twist. It's the reminder that being underestimated is not a weakness a man has to correct loudly — the correction can just as easily be a quiet accumulation of results, delivered so calmly the other party doesn't notice they've lost the argument until it's already over.

title: GTA 6 Netflix Premiere: Why Rockstar Chose Netflix First
stand: Twenty-seven minutes of gameplay, TV-MA rated, went to Netflix subscribers before it touched Rockstar's own channels. That isn't a marketing accident — it's a company that knows exactly what its attention is worth.

hero.alt: Jason Duval and Lucia Camino leaning against a green sports car in front of a Vice City skyline in Grand Theft Auto VI

body: On August 27, the biggest single reveal in Grand Theft Auto VI's entire run-up didn't premiere on Rockstar's YouTube channel, on a livestream, or at a press event. It premiered on Netflix. "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look" — twenty-seven minutes, TV-MA, built entirely from in-game PlayStation 5 footage — went out to Netflix subscribers worldwide first, in thirteen subtitle languages, before it touched any channel Rockstar actually owns.
IMG::0
IMG::1

That's not a distribution accident. "Grand Theft Auto reveals have become cultural moments in their own right," said Brandon Riegg, Netflix's VP of Nonfiction Series, on the release. "The anticipation and fandom around Grand Theft Auto VI is unprecedented, and we're honored that Rockstar Games has partnered with us to debut the next part of the Grand Theft Auto story with Netflix members first." Read plainly, that's a streaming platform admitting a video game reveal was a bigger get than most of its own original programming.
PQ::A studio handed its biggest reveal to a platform that has never shipped a game, because that platform could put it in front of more people on day one than Rockstar's own channels could.

The footage itself finally puts faces to the story that's been theorized for years: Jason Duval and Lucia Camino, two people who've always known the deck is stacked against them, watch an easy score go wrong and end up on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America — a criminal conspiracy stretching across the fictional state of Leonida. It's Rockstar's first extended, official look at how the world actually plays, after years of frame-by-frame trailer forensics standing in for real information.
IMG::2
IMG::3

There's a tidy piece of symmetry buried in the timing. Grand Theft Auto VI arrives thirteen years after Grand Theft Auto V — almost the exact span Netflix has spent building itself from a DVD-mail service into the company now capable of premiering a game reveal to a bigger simultaneous audience than any platform built for games. Two industries that didn't compete in 2013 are now trading favors over who gets to control the biggest reveal in entertainment.
VIDEO::0

None of this changes the actual bet Rockstar has been making for over a decade, which is that scarcity is the marketing. Going quiet for years only works if the silence gets filled by everyone else's theorizing instead of your own content — and the Netflix placement is really the same instinct at a different scale: instead of feeding the anticipation piecemeal across owned channels, hand the single largest piece of it to whoever can put it in front of the most people at once, then let Rockstar's own channels catch up after.
IMG::4

A second trailer followed the Netflix debut on Rockstar's own channels, closer to the conventional rollout — proof the studio isn't abandoning its usual playbook, just willing to open with someone else's audience when the moment calls for it.
VIDEO::1

Grand Theft Auto VI is set for November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, pre-orders open now. Whether thirteen years of theorizing survives contact with the actual game is a separate, honest question — expectation this large has broken plenty of releases before it. But as a lesson in knowing exactly what your own attention is worth, and refusing to spend it anywhere smaller than necessary, the Netflix debut alone is worth studying.

title: Why Drake's ICEMAN Album Is Still On Repeat, Months Later
stand: Some albums get a week. This one got moved into the rotation permanently, and nobody in the room has asked to change it since.

hero.alt: Official cover art for Drake's album Iceman

body: Most albums, even good ones, get roughly two weeks of genuine attention before they quietly slide into the back catalog — played occasionally, referenced fondly, but no longer the thing actually queued up on a given night. Drake's Iceman didn't follow that pattern here, and it's worth asking honestly why, instead of just noting that it happened.

Part of it is pacing. An album built for genuine repeat listening has to reward attention on the fifth pass the same way it rewarded it on the first, which is a much harder trick than making a strong first impression. Most records front-load their best material and let the back half coast; this one keeps giving the listener a reason to stay through the whole runtime, which is the actual test of whether something belongs in permanent rotation or just a good first week.
PQ::Some albums get a week. This one got moved into the rotation permanently.

There's also something to be said for an album that holds up as background and as foreground equally well — playing during a working afternoon without demanding attention, and holding up just as well at higher volume with actual focus on it later that night. That range is rarer than it should be, and it's the difference between an album you like and an album you live with.

It plays on repeat in a specific room here, alongside a certain British crime picture that never seems to leave the rotation either — two very different things sharing screen and speaker time simply because neither one has worn out its welcome yet, months in. That's a higher bar than most culture clears, and most of what clears it does so quietly, without campaign.

None of this is a lyric-by-lyric breakdown, on purpose — the specifics of what's actually being said belong to the person who wrote it, and repeating them here would miss the point of what actually makes an album worth this kind of loyalty anyway. It isn't any single line. It's the cumulative effect of an album built to survive familiarity instead of relying on novelty to carry it.

Most music gets judged in its first week and forgotten by its third. The real test — the only one that actually matters months later — is whether it's still getting chosen on a night when literally anything else in the catalog was available instead. This one keeps getting chosen, and at some point that stops being a coincidence and starts being the whole review.

body: Summer's over, the Living Floor screen has opinions about it, and the month ahead is stacked enough that a shortlist is doing you a favor. Two Guy Ritchie properties come back in the same three weeks, a brewery dynasty gets the Steven Knight treatment, and a horror franchise starts over with a director who's earned the trust. Here's what's actually worth the remote.

The Gentlemen — Season 2 — Netflix, Sept 3
Theo James and Kaya Scodelario are a year further into the family business, which means the problems have gotten bigger along with the ambition. This is the show already living on the Living Floor screen for good reason — the tone hasn't softened and a third season is already locked, so there's no reason to wait on this one.

The Death of Robin Hood — In theaters
Hugh Jackman playing the legend as someone actually worn down by the life, opposite Jodie Comer and Bill Skarsgård as Little John, is a more interesting proposition than another men-in-tights retread. The pitch is a harder, more honest version of a story everyone thinks they already know.
VIDEO::1

Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger — UK cinemas this month, Disney+ after
The Gallagher brothers in the same room, on camera, for the first joint interview in over two decades — that alone is the whole pitch. Whatever's actually in the documentary is almost beside the point next to the fact that it exists at all.
VIDEO::2
PQ::Two Guy Ritchie properties in the same three weeks is either a coincidence or a statement. Either way, clear the calendar.

MobLand — Season 2 — Paramount+, Sept 18
Tom Hardy, Pierce Brosnan, and Helen Mirren picking the fight back up, released weekly instead of dumped all at once — a rare bit of patience from a streamer, and the right call for a show built on slow-building dread rather than binge momentum.
VIDEO::3

House of Guinness — Netflix — catch up before the next one
If last year's release window buried this one under everything else Netflix put out, September is the correction. Steven Knight's take on the family behind the brewery, four siblings and one inheritance nobody agrees on — it's the kind of prestige-drama scheming that rewards a proper sit-down, not background viewing.
VIDEO::4

The Damned United — A rewatch worth making room for
Michael Sheen's Brian Clough during the infamous 44 days at Leeds United is one of the better performances of ego and self-sabotage put on film, football fan or not. Peter Morgan wrote it, which tells you the dialogue is doing as much work as the football.
VIDEO::5

Resident Evil — UK cinemas, Sept 18
Zach Cregger built his reputation on knowing exactly how long to hold a shot before something goes wrong, which makes him a genuinely interesting choice for this. It's a new story rather than a retread of the games, which is either a risk or the only way this was ever going to work.
VIDEO::6
Pull up a chair, pour something worth pouring, and work through it in whatever order the week allows.

title: Why Is Nike Leaving the S&P 100? The Real Reason, Explained
stand: It isn't a delisting, and Nike isn't going anywhere. But a company doesn't lose its seat among the hundred biggest names in America without the market saying something about why.

hero.alt: A Nike storefront sign beside a financial district stock ticker board showing the S&P 100 index, illustrating Nike's removal from the index

meta_description: Nike exits the S&P 100 on September 21, 2026, replaced by Dell, Palo Alto Networks, Arista and SanDisk. What the quarterly index rebalance actually means — and what it doesn't.
body: Before U.S. markets open on September 21, 2026, Nike will lose its seat in the S&P 100. Read quickly, that sentence sounds like the kind of thing that precedes a eulogy. Read correctly, it's an index-membership change — a piece of financial bookkeeping, not a verdict on whether the company survives the decade.

The mechanics are almost boring, which is the point. S&P Dow Jones Indices announced the change on September 4 as part of its routine quarterly rebalance. Nike exits alongside Honeywell Aerospace, Simon Property Group, and Colgate-Palmolive. Dell Technologies, Palo Alto Networks, Arista Networks, and SanDisk move in. Four consumer-adjacent and industrial names out, four infrastructure-and-security names in — a rotation, not a purge.
PQ::This is a change to index membership. It is not an announcement that Nike's shares stop trading.

The S&P 100 exists to track roughly a hundred of the largest, most liquid companies in the country — a narrower cut of the broader S&P 500, rebalanced periodically so the list stays honest about who's actually big right now, not who used to be. That's the entire mechanism. It doesn't ask whether a company is well run, only how much of it the market currently believes exists.

By that measure, Nike's answer has gotten smaller. The stock has fallen more than three-quarters from its 2021 peak, and the math behind that decline is not abstract — by some estimates it has erased on the order of $230 billion in market value, with shares recently trading near levels the company hasn't seen in roughly twelve years. Losing a seat reserved for the hundred largest companies in America is simply what happens to the math when the number underneath it shrinks that far.

What it isn't is a delisting. Nike remains a full constituent of the S&P 500, the index most retirement accounts and index funds actually track, and its shares keep trading exactly as they did the day before. A fund built to hold the broad market has no reason to touch its Nike position because of this change alone. The only funds forced to act are the ones built specifically to track the narrower hundred — and even there, the selling is mechanical, timed to the effective date, and over almost as soon as it starts.

The more honest read is the symbolic one. Nike held its place in the S&P 100 for nearly eighteen years — long enough that an entire generation of investors never saw the index without it. All four names replacing it come from the same direction: chips, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity. That's not a coincidence so much as a receipt. It's where the market has decided the next decade of American corporate weight is actually sitting, and it isn't sitting in a swoosh.

None of which makes this nothing. For a company mid-turnaround, getting quietly moved out of the room reserved for the hundred biggest names in the country is the kind of marker that shows up in board memos long before it shows up in a press release. It just isn't the marker most people will assume it is when they see the headline — and the difference between those two readings is usually where the actual information lives.

title: Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari F40: The Story Behind His Rarest Car
stand: The engine block was stamped 44 before Hamilton ever owned it. He just spent three decades becoming the one man alive for whom that would count as fate.

hero.alt: Lewis Hamilton in a camel overcoat and beret standing beside his Ferrari F40, its yellow UK-style number plate reading 44, surrounded by photographers at the 2026 Italian Grand Prix

meta_description: Lewis Hamilton arrived at the 2026 Italian Grand Prix in a restored, ultra-low-mileage Ferrari F40 — its engine block stamped 44, his own racing number, found by accident during a factory restoration in Maranello.
body: The Ferrari F40 has never needed an introduction, which made it the strangest possible car to arrive somewhere quietly. Lewis Hamilton rolled into Monza for the 2026 Italian Grand Prix behind the wheel of one anyway, in a black pinstripe suit, tie, and beret, a camel overcoat draped over his shoulders in ninety-degree heat, stepping out of a supercar with no air conditioning like the temperature was somebody else's problem. Photographers who arrive expecting a paddock story sometimes leave with a fashion story instead. This was both.

The car earning that entrance wasn't a showroom pull. It's a European-market F40 whose first and only owner reportedly drove it 69 kilometers from Maranello before parking it for good — the passenger door, by Hamilton's account, never opened again until he owned it. Three decades in storage left the original factory red paint thin enough that the carbon fiber and Kevlar weave underneath still shows through, which is precisely the kind of imperfection a serious collector chases and a casual one paints over.
IMG::0
IMG::1

Hamilton sent it to Ferrari's own Classiche division in Maranello rather than a private restorer — a recommissioning, in his words, not a restomod. The distinction matters more than it sounds: a restomod improves on the original; a recommissioning simply wakes it back up, wiring and fluids and three-decade-old rubber brought current without touching the parts that make the car worth waking up in the first place.

It was mid-teardown that Ferrari's mechanics found the detail nobody was looking for: the engine block stamped with the number 44. Hamilton's number. Stamped at the factory in the late 1980s, decades before a driver who'd make it his own had been born to a father whose own Vauxhall Cavalier carried that plate while a young Hamilton was still karting. The car had been sitting on that coincidence since before he existed to appreciate it.
PQA::The engine had 44 on it. I didn't put that there.||Lewis Hamilton||
IMG::2

None of which would matter as much if the car underneath the coincidence weren't what it is. The F40 was the last road car Enzo Ferrari personally approved before his death in 1988 — the final word from a man who spent his life deciding what counted as a real Ferrari, delivered as a raw, largely unassisted, twin-turbocharged argument that lightness and power mattered more than comfort ever would.

SPEC::{"model": "FERRARI F40", "rows": [["Engine", "2.9L Twin-Turbocharged V8"], ["Max Power", "471 HP"], ["0-60 MPH", "3.9 SEC"], ["Top Speed", "201 MPH"], ["Kerb Weight", "~2,425 LBS"], ["Body", "Composite Over Tubular Steel"], ["Production", "1,311 Units (1987\u20131992)"], ["Approved By", "Enzo Ferrari, 1987"]], "cta_label": "", "cta_url": "", "cta_title": "", "image": null}

Hamilton hasn't said what he paid, and pristine F40 values move on originality and mileage more than on any fixed number — a 1,118-mile example changed hands for €4.3 million in 2026. A 69-kilometer car that spent thirty years with one unopened door sits closer to the top of that range than the middle of it, though the honest answer is that a car this specific doesn't have a clean comparable.
IMG::3
IMG::4

What actually separates this from a celebrity buying a nice old Ferrari is the order of operations. He didn't commission a plate to match his number, or ask a shop to stamp something meaningful onto the block. The car came that way, waited three decades to be found that way, and ended up in the one garage in the world where it would mean something. That's a harder thing to buy than the car was.

title: Christopher Nolan's New Movie Won't Leave IMAX. Here's Why That Matters.
stand: Eleven weeks in, on a format only forty-one screens on Earth can even show, audiences keep choosing the harder way to watch a movie. That's either stubbornness or the entire argument for theaters at all.

hero.alt: Matt Damon as Odysseus leading armored soldiers off a beached ship in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey

meta_description: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey extends its IMAX 70mm run through September 30, 2026 — an 11th week on a format shown in only 41 theaters worldwide, as the film becomes Nolan's highest-grossing release and the top-grossing R-rated movie ever.
body: Homer's Odyssey is a story about a journey that refuses to end on schedule. Every time Odysseus gets close to home, something extends the trip — a god, a storm, an island he can't quite leave. Nolan's version has managed the same trick at the box office. What was supposed to close on September 15 is now booked through September 30, its eleventh week on a format that exists in exactly forty-one theaters worldwide.
IMG::0
IMG::1

That format is the detail worth sitting with. IMAX 70mm is not the same thing as "IMAX," and it is definitely not the same thing as "IMAX with Laser" — it is actual 70-millimeter film, threaded through a handful of projectors built for it, in rooms most people will never stand in. Universal and Nolan didn't extend the wide release. They extended the hardest version of this movie to see, because that is the version people kept showing up for.
PQ::They extended the hardest version of this movie to see, because that's the one people kept showing up for.

The numbers explain why nobody wanted to be the studio that closed it early. The Odyssey has pulled in $457 million worldwide on IMAX screens alone, a record that doesn't just beat Avatar's decade-old $271 million mark — it beats it by more than the entire theatrical run of most films released this year. The 70mm engagements, all forty-one of them, have generated $66 million on their own: a $1.6 million average per screen, at a $20.58 average ticket, in a pair of months that are now the two highest-grossing in IMAX's history.
IMG::2

Zoom out from the premium formats and the film's regular math is just as absurd. $1.55 billion worldwide makes The Odyssey the second-highest-grossing release of the year, Nolan's highest-grossing film ever — ahead of The Dark Knight Rises' $1.1 billion — and the highest-grossing R-rated movie of all time, a record it took from Deadpool & Wolverine's $1.338 billion. It did all of that as a three-hour, R-rated adaptation of a three-thousand-year-old poem, which is not the description of anything a studio's spreadsheet would have bet on.

The cast carries its own version of the same story. Matt Damon's Odysseus, Anne Hathaway's Penelope, Robert Pattinson, and Samantha Morton's Circe are each posting the highest-grossing release of their careers, which says less about any single performance than about what happens when a director spends two decades convincing audiences that the room matters as much as the screen.
IMG::3

That's the actual case being made here, eleven weeks in. A theatrical release competing with a phone in every pocket doesn't win by being merely available — it wins by being worth a specific trip, to a specific room, in a format you have to look for on purpose. Most people asking for "IMAX tickets" will end up in a room that isn't running film at all. The ones checking for the words "70mm" next to the listing are the ones this extension was for.
The run ends September 30, assuming nothing extends it again. Given the pattern so far, betting against one more delay would be a very Odyssey mistake to make.

title: The Balvenie Waited 88 Years. Daniel Arsham Built the Proof.
stand: Cask #239 was filled in 1931 and opened in 2019. Nobody currently on staff at the distillery was alive for either date. Seventeen decanters is what that patience becomes.

hero.alt: Daniel Arsham's sculptural vessel for The Balvenie's 88-Year-Old whisky, set into a raked sand spiral forming the number 88

meta_description: Daniel Arsham built a bronze, copper, and oak sculpture to house The Balvenie's 88-Year-Old — the oldest whisky ever released — debuting at Frieze Seoul with an immersive barley-floor performance, 'Dawn Of Our Spirit.'
body: Cask #239 was filled at The Balvenie's Speyside distillery in 1931. It was opened in 2019, eighty-eight years later, by Malt Master Kelsey McKechnie. Nobody currently working at the distillery was alive for either date. What came out was enough for seventeen decanters, and the whole story of what that kind of patience is actually worth.
IMG::0
IMG::1

The Balvenie built its new 1931 Collection around that cask, and rather than launch it like a product, the label handed the debut to Daniel Arsham as a live installation at Frieze Seoul. "Dawn Of Our Spirit" puts four dancers inside a circular bed of loose barley at S50 in Seongsu, their choreography — by Sukyung Yoo — echoing the slow, repetitive labor of turning grain on a malting floor by hand. A soundscape recorded inside the actual Speyside distillery plays underneath it, so the room doesn't read as a gallery so much as an abstracted version of the working floor eighty-eight years removed.

Arsham traces the project back to his first trip to Speyside. "One of the things that struck me was the handmade quality of everything. It's technical, but very craft in a way, so I pulled out a lot of materials I saw," he said, sitting across from a table of early, discarded mockups. "In the end, the preciousness of that liquid really needs to be considered."
IMG::2

That consideration shows up as an object built almost entirely out of metaphor. The whisky itself sits in a hand-blown crystal decanter detailed with 18-karat gold, its neck shaped after the "Balvenie Ball" — the distillery's distinctively shaped still, and the source of the whisky's honeyed character. Arsham's housing around it splits into three materials, each standing in for a stage of the maturation: eight hand-patinated bronze layers on the front, one for each decade the cask spent waiting; a copper disc at the center, cast from a retired still; and eighty-eight thin layers of oak across the back, one per year, referencing the European sherry butt the spirit first went into.
IMG::6
IMG::7
PQ::It's the whisky when it's moving through time. It's moving through the copper, into the wood, and then into your glass.||Daniel Arsham||
IMG::3

1931 wasn't only the year the cask was filled. It's also the year The Balvenie opened its Home Malt Floor, which the distillery still operates today — one of a handful in Scotland stubborn enough to keep hand-turning barley in an industry that automated the process decades ago. The performance isn't really staging something symbolic; it's staging the one part of the process that hasn't changed since the cask it's honoring was filled.

After the barley settles, the experience moves into a gallery holding Arsham's sculpture alongside guided tastings led by McKechnie herself. "It's still a very handmade process," Arsham said of the decision to build an entire performance around it. "Sometimes we lose a little bit of that seeing it just on a shelf or having it at home. We tried together to bring some of that into the experience and tell that story."

The fit makes sense once you know Arsham's broader practice. He calls it "fictional archaeology" — treating ordinary, often industrial objects as artifacts recovered from some future excavation, carrying centuries of imagined wear. A whisky that spent eighty-eight years becoming what it is barely needed the fiction.
IMG::4

"In whisky, nothing happens overnight," McKechnie said. "The fruits of today's craftspeople might not be tasted for generations. Being able to release an 88-year-old really reaffirms this to everyone at the distillery — that all the hard work we're putting in today is a real testament to persistence and patience. That's something I think Daniel understands beautifully."

The 88-year-old is now the oldest whisky ever released, a record The Balvenie doesn't seem interested in treating quietly. "At The Balvenie, we are always in charge of our own destiny," McKechnie said. "I love the thought of us doing something that changes the landscape of Scotch whisky. We've done it before. I relish the opportunity to do it again."
IMG::5

"Dawn Of Our Spirit" continues on to New York, Shanghai, and Taipei after Seoul. Seventeen decanters will outlast the tour, the distillery, and most of the people who see the performance — which was more or less the point of filling the cask in 1931 in the first place.

title: A. Lange & Söhne 1815 UP/DOWN (2026): What Actually Changed
stand: Anyone can add a color. Only a handful of manufactures on earth can shrink a case by a millimeter and a half without the watch losing an ounce of what made it serious in the first place.

hero.alt: A. Lange & Söhne's new 1815 UP/DOWN in white gold and pink gold, both with deep blue dials, side by side

meta_description: A. Lange & Söhne debuts a smaller, blue-dialed 1815 UP/DOWN and a platinum TRIPLE SPLIT with a rhodié dial at the 2026 Concours of Elegance — what actually changed, and why the size reduction matters more than the color.
body: A. Lange & Söhne used the 2026 Concours of Elegance at Hampton Court Palace to extend two of its most established families, and the headline detail in both press photos is the same: a blue dial, a platinum case, the kind of thing that reads well in a product shot. The actual news is quieter than that, and it's the kind of quiet that only a handful of manufactures on earth can afford to make the whole story.
IMG::0
IMG::1

Start with the 1815 UP/DOWN, because the real change isn't the color. The previous generation of this watch measured 39mm across. The new white-gold and pink-gold editions — references 244.028 and 244.037, 300 pieces each — bring that down to 37.5mm, while holding the case at exactly the same 8.7mm thickness and keeping the identical L051.2 caliber inside it. A millimeter and a half sounds like nothing until you consider what most watchmakers do instead when they want a release to feel new: bigger case, busier dial, a complication nobody asked for. Lange went the other direction, on purpose, and it's a harder trick to pull off than adding anything would have been.
PQ::Lange didn't modernize this watch with a sportier bracelet or a busier dial. It modernized it by taking something away.

The dial does its own work, too — a solid dark blue face against argenté-toned sub-dials, blued steel for the power-reserve and seconds hands, gold hands matched to the case for the hours and minutes. It's a sharper, more contemporary read on a design that's stayed close to Ferdinand Adolph Lange's original pocket-watch layout for over a century, and the contrast makes a genuinely classical watch feel intentional rather than simply heritage-coded.
IMG::2

The mechanism behind the name is where Lange's actual argument lives. "UP/DOWN" refers to the AUF (wound) and AB (unwound) indicator sitting opposite the seconds sub-dial, and rather than bolting a power-reserve module onto an existing movement — the shortcut most of the industry takes — Lange built the indication directly into the L051.2 caliber through a compact planetary-gear system. The movement is hand-wound, assembled twice per Lange's standard practice, and delivers 72 hours on a single wind. The feature is native to the mechanism, not added to it, which is precisely the distinction serious collectors are paying for.

There's a menswear read here too, if you're the type to think that way. The white gold is the cooler, more architectural version — built for navy tailoring, charcoal flannel, minimalist black eveningwear. The pink gold runs warmer, and does more with brown, tobacco, cream, and olive. Neither is the safer choice. They're just arguing for different rooms.
IMG::3

Alongside the 1815, Lange also extended the TRIPLE SPLIT — still, since its 2018 debut, the only mechanical chronograph in the world able to measure comparative and intermediate times across seconds, minutes, and hours simultaneously, up to a combined twelve-hour span. It's a complication built for exactly one problem most people will never have — timing two runners across a marathon, say, without losing either split — solved with a level of mechanical overkill that borders on the theatrical.

The new platinum edition dresses that complication in a cool rhodié dial against dark grey auxiliary counters, luminous main hands, and blued rattrapante hands that only reveal themselves mid-split. The 43.2mm 950-platinum case is fitted to a dark brown alligator strap on a platinum deployant buckle, and the whole edition is capped at 100 pieces.
IMG::4

Turn it over and the case for the price becomes a lot more literal. The hand-wound L132.1 caliber inside is built from 567 finished components — untreated German silver bridges, Glashütte ribbing, a hand-engraved balance cock, five gold chatons — plus a patented disengagement mechanism that eliminates friction loss the instant the rattrapante hands stop. Nobody buying this watch needs to time two marathon splits at once. They're buying the fact that the mechanism exists to do it without compromise, whether or not it's ever asked to.
IMG::5
Neither release adds a complication nobody asked for or a size nobody wanted. Both do the harder, less photogenic thing: refine a design that already worked, and let the restraint be the news.

title: Michael Jordan's Lost Ferrari 550 Maranello Is Going to Auction
stand: Michael Jordan drove it out of the United Center the night he won his fifth title. Tinker Hatfield had already put it on a shoe by the time anyone noticed it was gone.

hero.alt: Front view of Michael Jordan's customized 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello with headlights on, heading to auction at JOOPITER

meta_description: Michael Jordan's customized 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello — the car that inspired the Air Jordan XIV and vanished for 24 years — heads to JOOPITER's first-ever car auction, estimated at $700,000 to $1.3 million.
body: On June 13, 1997, Michael Jordan drove a Ferrari 550 Maranello out of the United Center with an Illinois vanity plate reading "MJ 5," hours after clinching his fifth championship. A year later, Nike's Tinker Hatfield put that same car's bodywork onto a basketball shoe. Then, at the end of 2002, Jordan sold it — and for twenty-four years, nobody outside a private garage knew where it was.
IMG::0
IMG::1

It resurfaced in early 2026, tracked down by the Miami dealer Curated, and it's now heading to auction through JOOPITER — the collectibles platform Pharrell Williams founded — in the company's first-ever car sale. Chassis 108712 goes to online bidding September 15 through 30, with a pre-sale estimate of $700,000 to $1.3 million. Even the low end of that range already exceeds the standing public-auction record for a stock 550 Maranello, which tells you exactly how much of the number is Ferrari and how much of it is Jordan.

The car itself was never stock. Delivered in May 1997 in Rosso Barchetta over chrome Speedline wheels, it hides a naturally aspirated 485-hp V12 behind a gated manual transmission — the purist's configuration, on a car built for a man who could have specified anything. Ferrari extended the seat rails and slimmed the padding to fit Jordan's 6-foot-6 frame, and at his request, built it without the yellow fender shields every other 550 wore. Everyone else's Ferrari announced itself. His didn't need to.
IMG::2

The plate is the part collectors will actually be bidding on. "MJ 5" wasn't added for the auction — it was on the car the day he drove it out of the arena, and it's still there. The 550 also turns up rolling out of a January 1998 practice in The Last Dance, which means its screen time predates the documentary that made everyone else's Jordan memorabilia valuable by two decades.
PQ::Everyone else's Ferrari announced itself. His didn't need to.

What actually separates this specific car from any other well-provenanced Jordan artifact is that it didn't just witness the era — it designed part of it. Nike's Tinker Hatfield used the 550 as a direct reference for the Air Jordan XIV: the shoe's low, aerodynamic side profile echoes the car's body line, its lateral vents reference the Ferrari's side intakes, and its shield-shaped Jumpman mark was built as a basketball-world answer to the prancing horse on the hood. Even the tread pattern on the outsole reads as a motorsport cue. It's one of the cleanest examples in sneaker history of a personal object becoming a design language, rather than a brand bolting a car reference on after the fact.
IMG::3

Jordan debuted the Air Jordan XIV on June 14, 1998 — Game 6 of the Finals against Utah, the night of "The Last Shot," his final basket as a Chicago Bull and the sixth championship. JOOPITER is pairing this sale with Jordan's game jersey from that same series, estimated separately at $10 million to $15 million, under a deliberate "Driven to Greatness" framing: the car, the shoe it designed, and the jersey from the game the shoe was designed for.

None of that required the car to actually be driven much. It shows just under 19,000 miles after twenty-nine years, most of them spent doing nothing more dramatic than sitting somewhere out of view. That's the real shape of the story: an object famous enough to redesign a sneaker and anchor a documentary spent most of its life being invisible, and is about to spend two weeks in September being the most examined car in the country. Preview runs September 15 through 20 at CART Department in New York, for anyone who wants to see the plate in person before the bidding decides what it's actually worth.

title: Stephen Curry Wants to Retire a Warrior. The NBA's Rulebook Gets a Vote Too.
stand: Curry saying he wants to finish his career in Golden State isn't the story — everyone already assumed that. The story is a rule most fans have never heard of, quietly deciding how long that promise can legally be written.

hero.alt: Stephen Curry walking toward cheering fans reaching for autographs and jerseys after a Golden State Warriors game

body: Stephen Curry telling NBC Sports Bay Area and ABC7 that he expects to finish his career with the Golden State Warriors isn't really news. Nobody watching the Warriors for the last decade seriously entertained another ending. The actual story sitting underneath that headline is a rule almost no fan could name, quietly deciding how long that promise is even allowed to be written down.
IMG::0

Curry enters the final year of his current deal in 2026-27 at $62.6 million, which makes him the league's highest-paid player this season on an annual basis, extension or not. He's also eligible right now for a two-year max extension worth up to $136.7 million. Both of those numbers are real. Neither of them is the constraint actually shaping the decision.

That constraint is the NBA's Over-38 Rule, and it doesn't ask whether the Warriors want to keep Curry or whether he wants to stay — both of those questions are already settled. What it limits is how long a new contract is allowed to run once a player crosses that age threshold: no more than three total years under contract from the point the rule kicks in. It exists to stop teams and players from using long, back-loaded deals in a player's late thirties to quietly shift cap obligations into the future. It was never built to end anyone's career on a timer; it just forces the paperwork into shorter increments.
IMG::1
IMG::2
PQ::The rule doesn't ask whether the Warriors want to keep him. It asks how the contract is allowed to be shaped.

That leaves Curry two real paths, and both of them still end in Golden State. He can sign the two-year, $136.7 million extension now, which locks in certainty through 2028-29 — his age-40 season — and takes any contract talk off the table before it can distract a team that needs every advantage it can get. Or he can play out this season, hit free agency, and negotiate a fresh contract instead of an extension, reportedly worth as much as $207 to $213 million over three years, stretching into his age-42 season. More total money, more years, and a bet that his body cooperates long enough to collect on it.

Golden State's front office isn't hedging on which ending it expects. General manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. has said he's "pretty confident" Curry finishes his career as a Warrior, and the organization's position is straightforward: he wants to stay, they want him to stay, and the timing gets built around what actually works for him.

None of this happens in a vacuum of good health. Curry played just 43 games in 2025-26, and Golden State went out in the play-in tournament without ever fielding a fully healthy roster. Whatever ceiling this retooled group — Jimmy Butler, Draymond Green, Kristaps Porziņģis — is actually capable of reaching depends entirely on Curry being available to reach it, extension or not.

Four championships, two MVPs, eleven All-NBA selections, twelve All-Star appearances, a spot on the NBA's 75th Anniversary Team, and eighteen seasons in one uniform is the kind of résumé that used to be common in this league and is now nearly extinct. The genuinely modern part of the story isn't that Curry wants to be a one-team player. It's that finishing as one now runs through a rule most of the league's own fans have never had to think about — proof that even the most sentimental ending in sports still has to clear a legal department first.

title: Tupac Shakur Murder Verdict: Duane "Keffe D" Davis Found Guilty, Explained
stand: Duane "Keffe D" Davis never fired a shot. Nevada law didn't require that he had, and a Las Vegas jury needed less than three hours to agree.

hero.alt: Split image of Duane "Keffe D" Davis in custody in a Las Vegas courtroom beside an archival photo of Tupac Shakur

meta_description: A Las Vegas jury convicted Duane "Keffe D" Davis of first-degree murder in Tupac Shakur's 1996 killing — the first conviction in the case in nearly 30 years, built almost entirely on Davis's own words.
body: A Las Vegas jury needed less than three hours to convict Duane "Keffe D" Davis of first-degree murder in the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur. It is the first conviction of any kind in a case that had gone unresolved for nearly thirty years — and prosecutors never once claimed Davis pulled the trigger.

That distinction is the legal foundation the entire case was built on. Under Nevada law, a person who helps direct or carry out a murder can be held as criminally responsible as the person who fires the shot. Prosecutors used that principle to present Davis, a 63-year-old former Compton gang figure, as the "shot caller" who supplied the weapon and set the retaliation in motion, rather than the man in the back seat who fired it. He is the only person ever charged in Shakur's death.

The outline of that night is well established. Shakur, 25, was shot in a drive-by attack near the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996, while riding in a car driven by Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight; he died of his injuries days later. Prosecutors argued the shooting followed an earlier fight at the MGM Grand, where Shakur and members of his group assaulted Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson — and that Davis, in response, obtained a gun and helped lead the search for Shakur that night.

What made the case unusual was what prosecutors didn't have. There was no recovered murder weapon, no recovered vehicle, no surveillance footage of the shooting, and no DNA or forensic evidence tying Davis directly to the scene. Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal built the case almost entirely on Davis's own words — 2008 and 2009 police interviews in which he described being in the car and passing a gun toward the back seat, his 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend, years of podcast and documentary appearances, and jail calls recorded after his 2023 arrest. In those accounts, spread across more than a decade, Davis had described his own role in the killing repeatedly and in detail.
IMG::0

The defense's response was that none of it should count as proof. Attorney Michael Sanft argued Davis had spent years exaggerating or fabricating his account to sell books and draw media attention, and called acquittal "the only verdict that makes sense in this case." A retired Las Vegas detective testified he couldn't independently verify parts of Davis's story, including hospital records for Anderson and rental records for the Cadillac Davis described. The jury heard roughly two dozen prosecution witnesses against three for the defense, and was not persuaded — returning a unanimous guilty verdict on a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon.
PQ::Prosecutors never claimed Davis fired the shots. Nevada law didn't require that he had.

The courtroom carried the weight of what the verdict actually closed. Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, wept as it was read. Davis's son covered his face. Davis himself stood silently through the decision, then raised a fist toward the gallery on his way out. District Judge Carli Kierny ordered him held without bail ahead of an October 13 sentencing, where he faces a maximum of life in prison; his attorneys have said they plan to appeal.

The case sat, from opening statements to verdict, inside the same East Coast–West Coast mythology that has shaped hip-hop's memory of the mid-1990s for a generation — The Notorious B.I.G.'s name surfaced repeatedly during the trial, a reminder of how inseparable the two deaths remain in the culture's telling of that era. Shakur's killing has been picked over by fans, journalists, and investigators for almost thirty years without a single conviction to show for it. As of Monday, for the first time, there is one.

title: Al Pacino & Anthony Hopkins' Maserati Movie: Everything We Know
stand: Al Pacino and Anthony Hopkins aren't playing Maseratis in this one. They're playing the money that decided whether the name survived long enough to mean anything.

hero.alt: Stylized key art from Maserati: The Brothers showing a vintage racing car speeding through a red-orange haze

meta_description: Maserati: The Brothers, starring Al Pacino and Anthony Hopkins, drops its first teaser — a founding-era racing biopic built around the marque's 1939-40 Indianapolis 500 wins, directed by Bobby Moresco.
body: Every carmaker eventually gets the reverent, present-tense treatment — the glossy heritage film that makes a factory floor look like a cathedral. "Maserati: The Brothers" isn't trying to be that. Its teaser, dropped August 31, spends its runtime on dust, narrow roads, and men risking a family business on cars that could kill them, which is a more honest place to start a story about a trident badge than a boardroom.
IMG::0
IMG::1

Director Bobby Moresco — the Oscar winner behind Crash's screenplay — is telling the founding story of Alfieri, Bindo, and Carlo Maserati, three brothers trying to turn an engineering obsession into a company that could survive contact with actual capitalism. The film's spine is the marque's back-to-back Indianapolis 500 wins in 1939 and 1940, driven by Wilbur Shaw in the 8CTF — the car that made Maserati a name worth defending rather than just a name worth trying.
IMG::2

The casting is where the film shows its hand. Al Pacino plays Vincenzo Vaccaro, an early investor betting real money on an unproven idea, and Anthony Hopkins plays Luca Antonelli, a financier shaping the business strategy behind the engineering. Neither man is playing a Maserati. Both are playing the kind of quiet, external leverage that decides whether an engineer's obsession becomes a company or just a very good story about a garage. Andy García and Jessica Alba round out the supporting cast, with Michele Morrone leading as Alfieri.
IMG::3

It was shot across Italy on purpose — Bologna, where the company was founded; Modena, where it still operates; and Rome's Cinecittà Studios for the rest — the same triangulated authenticity move Moresco already ran on Lamborghini: The Man Behind the Legend, and the same lineage of Italian-automotive biopics that includes Michael Mann's Ferrari. There's an emerging genre here, and this is its third entry in as many marques.
VIDEO::
IMG::4

A theatrical target of October 15, 2026 is circulating out of Italy, though reporting has consistently flagged that date as provisional rather than locked. What's already confirmed is the harder-edged pitch underneath the cast list: this isn't a supercar commercial dressed up as a period piece. It's a story about the years before the badge meant anything, when the only thing separating a great engineer from a bankrupt one was whether his car survived the next race — and whether the men bankrolling him were willing to find out.

title: Piaget Polo Minute Repeater (2026): Price, Specs, Why Only 5 Exist
stand: There's no stated final number, no "1 of 25" on the caseback. Five a year isn't a marketing cap — it's just how long the hand-finishing actually takes.

hero.alt: The Piaget Polo Minute Repeater in 18-karat white gold with a blue guilloché dial and blue textile strap

meta_description: Piaget's Polo Minute Repeater folds one of horology's hardest complications into an ultra-thin sport-chic case. Only five pieces are made per year — not a limited edition cap, but the actual limit of 50 hours of hand-finishing per watch.
body: "Only five pieces this year" reads like the standard scarcity line every watch brand reaches for eventually — a manufactured number designed to make a buyer move fast. Piaget's version of that sentence is different in a way that actually matters: there is no stated lifetime cap on the Polo Minute Repeater, no "1 of 25" waiting on the caseback. Five a year isn't a marketing ceiling. It's just how long the hand-finishing actually takes.
IMG::0

The watch itself is Piaget folding one of horology's hardest complications into a case that was never built to hide it. A minute repeater — a mechanism that chimes the time on demand, entirely acoustic, no battery involved — usually lives in a formal dress watch. Piaget put this one in the Polo, its modern sport-chic line, and left the caliber partially exposed through an openworked, guilloché dial instead of covering it up. The complication isn't a secret here. It's the point.

The case makes the argument for restraint on its own: 18-karat white gold, 48mm across but only 9.3mm thick, which is a genuinely difficult thinness to hit on a watch built to also ring a bell. Inside is the self-winding Caliber 1290P — 430 hand-finished components, entirely conceived, developed, and assembled at Piaget's La Côte-aux-Fées manufacture, spun by a platinum micro-rotor coated in blue PVD.
IMG::1

None of that finishing is decorative in the usual sense. A minute repeater lives or dies on acoustics, and Piaget engineered this one to chime the hours at G-sharp and the minutes at A-sharp in the fifth octave, at 64 decibels, triggered by a slide at 9 o'clock rather than a pusher. Every hand-beveled bridge and mirror-polished hammer inside is there to shape a sound most owners will only ever demonstrate to someone else in the room.
IMG::2

That's where the real math behind "five a year" comes from. The dial alone took over 150 hours to develop. Every individual watch then absorbs another 50 hours of hand-finishing before it's numbered and released. Piaget isn't deciding to make five. Five is what the calendar allows once you refuse to speed up either number.
IMG::3
IMG::4

The same movement gets a second, more ornamental life in a High Jewellery companion piece, reference G0A51017 — a fully openworked dial this time, set inside a bezel of baguette-cut blue sapphires and diamonds. It's the same 430-component argument underneath, just dressed for a different room.
IMG::5

The standard reference, G0A51038, is reported to retail around €330,000, available through Piaget boutiques on inquiry rather than a waitlist announcement. The more honest question isn't how many exist right now. It's how many years Piaget is willing to keep making exactly five.

title: Roger Federer's Hall of Fame Induction: His Full Speech, Explained
stand: Thirty minutes to describe his own career, and he spent most of it in tears over other people's names — his childhood hero, his coach, his wife. That's either deflection or the actual secret to what made him different.

hero.alt: Roger Federer smiling while holding the Wimbledon trophy

meta_description: Roger Federer was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame on August 29, 2026 — the 271st inductee, and the only player in the Class of 2026 alongside broadcaster Mary Carillo. Inside a speech built almost entirely around everyone but himself.
body: A Hall of Fame induction is structurally built to be about one person. The sport is formally agreeing that your name belongs in its permanent memory, and the entire ceremony exists to say so, at length, to your face. Roger Federer spent almost thirty minutes at Newport on August 29 doing something close to the opposite — turning his own induction speech into an accounting of everyone else's names.
IMG::0

He became the International Tennis Hall of Fame's 271st inductee, the sole player honoree in the Class of 2026, with broadcaster Mary Carillo entering alongside him in the contributor category. Mirka Federer introduced her husband, and he opened stripped of his usual composure: "Oh man. This is very high level and a tough act to follow." He admitted he'd been "a little stressed, to be honest," and then let the moment take over anyway.

What followed wasn't a highlight reel. It was closer to a ledger of debts. He broke down first over Stefan Edberg, the childhood hero whose game had pulled him toward tennis in the first place — what Federer called "happy tears" — then again over longtime coach Severin Luthi, and once more over Mirka, the sentence dissolving before he finished it. A man being inducted for what he did with a racket spent most of his speech on the people who taught him how.
IMG::1
PQ::A man being inducted for what he did with a racket spent most of his speech on the people who taught him how.

The record itself doesn't need defending, but it's worth having in one place: the first man to reach 20 Grand Slam singles titles, a record 237 consecutive weeks at world No. 1 out of 310 total, 10 straight major finals with 8 won, 8 Wimbledon titles, 6 Australian Opens, 5 consecutive US Opens from 2004 to 2008, and a lone French Open in 2009 that completed the career Grand Slam — a feat only eight men in the sport's history have managed. In 2006 alone he went 92-5 and won 12 titles, three of them majors, on his way to 23 consecutive Grand Slam semifinals and 36 straight major quarterfinals.

Rafael Nadal has since reached 22 majors and Novak Djokovic 24, and neither number takes anything from Federer's plaque. Being first to 20 and holding a 237-week unbroken run at No. 1 aren't records that get erased by someone else's later total — they're a different category of achievement entirely, the kind measured in duration and precedence rather than a final tally that anyone could eventually pass.
IMG::2

Mary Carillo's induction carried its own weight beside his. Billie Jean King, presenting her in the contributor category, put it plainly: "She has earned her spot in sports journalism and she has earned her spot in Newport." Carillo, 69, already a member of the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame, said the company she was joining was almost hard to believe.

Federer closed by thanking the ball boys who'd worked his matches and telling the next generation of players to push the game further than he had — a strange note to end on for the man being enshrined, and a fitting one for how he'd spent the previous half hour. "I'm thrilled to have made the journey here," he said. "To immerse yourself in the history of the sport means a lot to me." He's said before that fame was never the goal. Thirty minutes of a speech that was supposed to be about him, spent almost entirely on everyone else, is about as convincing as that claim is ever going to get.

title: Kith x adidas Samba "Denim": Release Info, Price, Details
stand: One shoe, two different stripe techniques on two different sides — pony hair on one, chain-stitch embroidery on the other. That mismatch is the actual design, not a flaw someone forgot to fix.

hero.alt: A pair of Kith for adidas Originals Samba 'Denim' sneakers side by side against a grey backdrop

meta_description: Kith and adidas Originals rework the Samba in bleached denim, pony hair, and chain-stitch embroidery — with deliberately mismatched Three Stripes on each side. Released August 31, 2026 at $120.
body: Most Samba collaborations solve the same problem the same way: swap in a premium leather, add a suede overlay, pick a bolder colorway, done. Kith's newest pass at the shoe skips that playbook entirely and treats the Samba like a garment instead of a sneaker — which is how you end up with a shoe whose two sides don't actually match, on purpose.
IMG::0

The "Denim" drops the usual leather-and-suede formula for bleached white and light-blue denim layered over a canvas base, with pony hair and chain-stitch embroidery doing the rest of the textural work. It released August 31 through Kith's stores, site, and app in New York, London, Paris, and Tokyo simultaneously, at $120 — the kind of release-day choreography that only makes sense once you've seen how much fabrication is actually happening on the upper.
IMG::1
IMG::2

The strongest idea in the shoe is the one detail most collaborations would have corrected: the Three Stripes don't match side to side. The lateral stripes are rendered in raised, luxe pony hair; the medial stripes are chain-stitch embroidery instead — two different techniques on two sides of the same shoe, deliberately mismatched rather than made consistent. It's a garment-design instinct applied to a sneaker: the kind of construction where a jacket might combine two different fabrications on purpose, rather than a shoe leaning on one loud logo or a single high-contrast colorway to make its point.
PQ::Two different techniques on two sides of the same shoe, deliberately mismatched rather than made consistent.
IMG::3

Branding stays quiet by comparison. A gold Kith script replaces the standard lateral "Samba" mark, the adidas Trefoil holds its usual place at the tongue, and the co-branding shows up again in smaller type across the tongue tag, heel, and footbed — present, but not fighting the materials for attention.
IMG::4

Everything underneath the denim stays exactly where the Samba archive says it should: cream laces, a padded collar, and the dark gum outsole that's been part of the shoe's vocabulary since long before anyone was layering pony hair onto it. That restraint is what keeps the silhouette legible under all the material experimentation — recognizable at ten feet, unfamiliar up close.
IMG::5

The styling case is that this isn't a blue sneaker so much as a textural neutral. Ecru denim, faded jeans, or relaxed khaki let the washes blend instead of clash; a navy knit, washed gray tee, cream overshirt, or canvas chore jacket echoes the palette without competing with it. Keep the rest of the fit similarly unbothered — high-saturation, ultra-clean pieces will fight the shoe's whole point, which is a washed, tactile finish that reads as slightly artisanal rather than manufactured. It's one of the more genuinely fashion-conscious Samba collaborations for exactly that reason: it makes an almost-too-familiar silhouette feel unfamiliar again without changing the shape anyone actually recognizes it by.

title: Vacheron Constantin Tribute to the Animal Kingdom: Inside the Six Watches
stand: Six artists who'd never built anything for a watch were handed a canvas smaller than a coin and about as much depth as a stack of index cards. None of them could just shrink their usual technique to fit.

hero.alt: All six watches from Vacheron Constantin's Metiers d'Art Tribute to the Animal Kingdom collection lined up side by side

meta_description: Vacheron Constantin's Metiers d'Art Tribute to the Animal Kingdom brings six outside artists -- working in feathers, glass, origami, embroidery, paper, and wood -- into a 4-millimeter space between dial and crystal. Here's how each of the six pieces was built.
body: Vacheron Constantin's "One of Not Many Crafts Programme" started with a straightforward premise: find six artists whose practices have nothing to do with watchmaking, and ask them to build something for a dial anyway. What made it hard wasn't the craft. Every one of these six people already knew how to work in their material. What none of them had ever done was work in it at a scale where the entire piece has to fit in roughly four millimeters of depth.

That number is the real subject of the Métiers d'Art Tribute to the Animal Kingdom collection. Each 42mm case — 12.9mm thick, in 18-karat white or 5N pink gold — leaves its six artisans about 3 to 4mm between the dial and the sapphire crystal to build an entire dimensional scene. None of them could simply shrink their studio technique to fit. Each had to invent a version of their craft that had never needed to exist before.

Julien Vermeulen's Feathersnake is the clearest case of that invention. His serpent is assembled from more than 200 individual pieces of goose feather and seven rare Lophophore feathers, cut and layered onto silk paper over a 3D metal appliqué until the scales catch light the way real iridescent plumage does. It's micro-plumasserie, a discipline built for millinery and costume work, rebuilt from scratch for a canvas smaller than a coin.
IMG::0

Simone Crestani's Glassoctopus takes the opposite material problem: instead of building up thin layers, he formed a transparent octopus from glass rods, worked dot by dot with tungsten tools until the creature rises just 3.5mm off a dark blue hand-guilloché gold dial.
IMG::1
IMG::2

Anja Midori's Oraygami solves the same depth problem in paper instead of glass — six manta rays, folded from self-dyed Japanese paper using micro-origami, suspended at different heights above a blue guilloché surface under a moiré-effect crystal so the rays appear to actually be swimming at depth.
IMG::3
IMG::4
PQ::None of them could simply shrink their studio technique to fit. Each had to invent a version of their craft that had never needed to exist before.
Laura Baverstock's Tigerbroidery embroiders a prowling tiger in 9-karat yellow and white gold thread and ceramic-coated copper wire onto green silk, mounted over a perforated titanium plate.
IMG::7
IMG::8

Marianne Guély's Papercroc goes monochrome entirely — an all-white crocodile in snow-like vegetation, laser-cut and heat-embossed from 250 and 300 gram cotton paper, a relief sculpture that happens to also tell time.
IMG::5
IMG::6

Anna Le Corno's Woodenwings closes the set with a falcon built from twelve wood species — circular background marquetry, sculptural layered marquetry, and a wing assembled feather by feather and cantilevered directly over the dial, the most physically ambitious construction of the six.
IMG::9
IMG::10

The mechanical foundation had to disappear behind all of it, which is its own quiet piece of engineering. Vacheron chose the Calibre 2460 G4 specifically because its four peripheral apertures display the hour, minute, day, and date without a single hand or central marker crossing the artwork — the movement gets out of the way on purpose. Every oscillating weight is hand-engraved in 22-karat gold with tool motifs referencing the specific artisan's own instruments, alongside a 40-hour power reserve and 3 bar of water resistance, with a calfskin strap embossed to echo whatever's happening on the dial above it.
IMG::11

None of the six pieces reach for the obvious version of their animal. The snake becomes an iridescent feather surface, the tiger a metallic-thread textile construction, the crocodile a monochrome paper relief, the falcon a study in wood grain, the manta rays a suspended paper choreography, the octopus a piece of transparent sculpture that happens to sit on a wrist. Vacheron's actual contribution here is closer to a gallery's than a manufacturer's — building the frame, choosing the constraint, and getting out of the way of six artists solving a problem none of them had faced before.

title: TRUNK(HOTEL) SAPPORO: Opening Date, Rooms, What to Know
stand: 107 rooms, a Michelin sushi counter, live music — and none of it is the actual reason to book. The reason is a 40-meter waterway on the 18th floor that TRUNK has never built before.

hero.alt: A TRUNK(HOTEL) SAPPORO suite at dusk with floor-to-ceiling views over the city

meta_description: TRUNK(HOTEL) SAPPORO opens September 17, 2027 as the brand's first property outside Tokyo -- 107 rooms in a Mid-Century Folklore design, anchored by TRUNK(BATH HOUSE), the brand's first spa, built around a 40-meter waterway and ten sensory bathing zones.
body: TRUNK(HOTEL) SAPPORO will have 107 rooms, a Michelin-recognized sushi counter, a chapel, a private cinema, and a live-music lounge when it opens September 17, 2027. None of that is the actual reason to book it. The reason is on the 18th floor: a 40-meter waterway that TRUNK has never built anything like before, in a spa concept the brand didn't previously have.

This is TRUNK's first property outside Tokyo — its fourth hotel overall, and by room count its largest — occupying floors 10 through 18 of the Sapporo Daibiru building in the city's central Odori district. The move outside Tokyo is itself the headline for a brand that built its identity there; everything about the property reads like a deliberate answer to the question of what TRUNK looks like somewhere else.
IMG::0

That answer is called "Mid-Century Folklore," designed by GENERAL DESIGN CO. with TRUNK Atelier. It isn't retro reproduction — it's mid-century restraint filtered through Hokkaido's own material culture: wood-centric textures, traditional handiwork, and finishes meant to keep a guest aware of the region's forests and climate despite being eighteen floors above a city center. The 89 standard rooms and 18 suites are the vehicle for that idea, not really the point of it.
IMG::1

The point is TRUNK(BATH HOUSE), the brand's first dedicated spa, built around an immersive "water utopia" rather than a conventional pool or a single public bath. Guests move through ten distinct bathing zones along the waterway, each engineered around a different combination of lighting, sound, and temperature — swimwear-friendly throughout, closer to a social urban bathhouse than a gender-segregated onsen.
IMG::2
IMG::3
PQ::None of that is the actual reason to book it. The reason is a 40-meter waterway TRUNK has never built anything like before.

The register shifts zone to zone on purpose — a rain-drenched jungle passage in one stretch, disco balls suspended over water in another, high-temperature sauna terracing lit from beneath each step, and quieter leather-lounger rooms built for the pause between the more theatrical spaces. Open-air baths complete the loop. It's designed as a sequence of contrasting conditions to move through, not a single wellness amenity to sit in.
IMG::4
IMG::5

Everything else in the building is genuinely strong and still plays a supporting role. The hotel's 10th-floor counter will be Sushi Saito's first Sapporo location, pairing the Michelin-recognized restaurant's Edo-mae technique with Hokkaido's own seafood, alongside all-day dining and a lounge bar with live music. A chapel opens straight onto forest for ceremonies, and a private studio handles cinema and karaoke on request.
IMG::6
IMG::7
IMG::8

Nightly rates are projected between ¥60,000 and ¥600,000 — roughly $375 to $3,755 — which places TRUNK(HOTEL) SAPPORO firmly in design-led luxury rather than mass boutique territory. A relatively small key count, a headline spa, and destination-level dining all pointing the same direction suggest TRUNK is building a cultural hub for the city rather than simply a place to sleep between days on the slopes.
IMG::9

TRUNK hasn't yet released the waterway's depth or temperature range, specific sauna capacities, whether bathhouse access is included for every room category, or a treatment menu — the kind of operational detail that typically surfaces closer to when reservations actually open. What's already clear is the bet underneath all of it: that a bathhouse, done seriously enough, can be the headline attraction of a hotel the way a view or a restaurant usually is.

title: Parmigiani Fleurier Tonda PF Skeleton Rose Gold: Price & Details
stand: Milano Blue debuted on platinum first, cool and monochrome. Move the same color onto rose gold and it stops being a finish and starts being a contrast.

hero.alt: The Parmigiani Fleurier Tonda PF Skeleton Rose Gold Milano Blue worn on the wrist

meta_description: Parmigiani Fleurier's 30-piece Tonda PF Skeleton Rose Gold Milano Blue moves an existing platinum colorway onto warm gold -- and changes its entire personality. Case, Calibre PF777 movement, and pricing detailed.
body: Parmigiani Fleurier didn't invent a new color for the Tonda PF Skeleton Rose Gold Milano Blue. Milano Blue already existed — it debuted on a platinum version of the same watch, where it read cool, monochrome, almost austere. Move that identical hue onto rose gold and it stops being a finish and starts being a contrast, which is the actual point of this 30-piece limited edition: proof that a color isn't fixed until you know what it's sitting next to.
IMG::0

The case carries the Tonda PF's established codes without needing to prove anything new: 40mm across, an 18-karat rose-gold build just 8.5mm thick, a finely knurled bezel, a screwed-in crown, and 100 meters of water resistance on an integrated rose-gold bracelet with a folding clasp. Sapphire crystals front and back leave nothing hidden.
IMG::1
IMG::2

What's actually hidden is nothing — that's the design premise. Parmigiani's approach to openworking here is architectural rather than technical for its own sake: components are selectively reduced to control proportion, light, and depth, not simply to show off how many parts a movement has. Warm rose gold on the case, hands, and applied indices; deep blue across the skeletonized bridges and dial architecture. The contrast is deliberate enough that it reads closer to navy tailoring paired with warm-toned accessories than to a conventional two-tone watch.
PQ::A color isn't fixed until you know what it's sitting next to.
IMG::3

Inside is the manufacture Calibre PF777 — automatic, 192 components, a 3.9mm profile, 29 jewels, running at 4Hz with a 60-hour power reserve. The satin-finished, hand-beveled bridges do the same architectural work as the case exterior, and the skeletonized 22-karat rose-gold rotor is built to integrate into that structure rather than sit on top of it as an obvious afterthought.
IMG::4
IMG::5

Each of the 30 pieces — reference PFC912-2020004-200182 — is individually numbered on the caseback, priced at CHF 97,000, roughly $117,100, through Parmigiani boutiques and authorized retailers. It's a small production run for what amounts to a genuinely disciplined idea: that the most convincing way to make an existing color feel new isn't to change the color at all, but to change what it's made of.
